verdict.reasoning: A verdict needs at least one positive observation of something behaving wrongly, and this board has none. The change log was never read, so deploy and config causes are untested rather than excluded [tr_7c7136d87842, tr_53f4cca39479]. The metric family queried for all four services does not exist for them, so no error, rate or latency delta is available anywhere [tr_ecf722d4c88a, tr_df4845357d16, tr_ff29c4182d6f, tr_0a142cfdc055]. The nginx log path — the one signal that separates freeze (silence), partition (cannot-reach messages), disk_fill (no space left) and bad_config (wrong address) — never executed, though Loki itself answered at the application layer and the query is recoverable [tr_ae542892c038]. The empty Tempo result [tr_3c7a09c7f07e] is the sole real observation, but it covers ~30 minutes preceding onset, which a fault starting at 05:12:35 could not have erased. Naming a mechanism from this would be invention.
verdict.root_cause: Not established. Nine of ten dispatches returned tool failures rather than measurements: all four change-history queries died with the same response-parse error [tr_7c7136d87842, tr_53f4cca39479, tr_f3ae6788e684, tr_06833e7a95d8], all four error-ratio baselines failed because span-derived metrics structurally do not exist for these services [tr_ecf722d4c88a, tr_df4845357d16, tr_ff29c4182d6f, tr_0a142cfdc055], and the nginx log query was rejected by Loki with HTTP 400 for a malformed pod matcher [tr_ae542892c038]. The only dispatch that actually observed its window found zero spans for nginx-web-server across 04:42:35-05:12:41 [tr_3c7a09c7f07e] — a window that is almost entirely before the 05:12:35 alert, so the silence fits a standing export gap (consistent with the Prometheus finding that this component emits no traces that become metrics) at least as well as an onset outage. No evidence here localises a failing mechanism to any of the four services.

alternatives.why_not: The only supporting datum is zero traces [tr_3c7a09c7f07e], and that gap covers ~30 minutes before onset, which a freeze starting at 05:12:35 cannot explain; the Prometheus results independently describe a standing telemetry gap for this component.
alternatives.root_cause: nginx-web-server stopped processing requests at onset while its socket still accepted, hanging callers and emitting nothing.

alternatives.why_not: Every change-history query failed on response parsing [tr_7c7136d87842, tr_53f4cca39479, tr_f3ae6788e684, tr_06833e7a95d8], so this is entirely unsupported speculation — plausible but with zero positive evidence behind it.
alternatives.root_cause: An unretrieved deploy or config change on one of the four services broke the request path at onset.

open_questions: What does nginx-web-server's own log say around 05:12:35? Re-run the Loki query with a corrected pod matcher — this one answer separates process_freeze, network_partition, disk_fill and bad_config.
Did nginx-web-server emit traces earlier in the day? If so, the empty window becomes incident evidence rather than an instrumentation gap.
What changed on any of the four services in the last 24 hours, and what signal actually fired the 05:12:35 alert?

draft.title: Front-door alert with no usable telemetry: an unresolved investigation

sections.body:
The page came from nginx-web-server, the front door of the social-network namespace. Severity was set critical and the declared blast radius covered four services: nginx-web-server itself plus the three backends it fans out to — compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service. Three of the edges between those services had never been measured before this incident, so there was no prior shape to compare against.

Read this record expecting disappointment. Ten dispatches went out; nine came back as tool failures rather than measurements, and the one that genuinely observed its window came back empty in a way that is ambiguous. Nothing below localises a failing mechanism. The value of this record is the map of which roads are closed and why.
sections.heading: What we were handed

sections.body:
The first real question was the obvious one for a fan-out service: which of the three downstream edges carries error status or inflated duration? The trace store was queried for nginx-web-server across roughly the thirty minutes ending at the alert.

It returned nothing. Not zero error spans — zero spans of any kind for the service across the whole window. That closed the per-dependency comparison immediately: with no spans at the service level, there is no edge data to rank, and narrowing or widening a status or peer filter cannot help, because the emptiness is not a filter artifact.

Two readings were available and the evidence does not choose between them. Either the service stopped processing requests, or its spans never reach the store. Worth noting the window geometry: it runs from about T-30m to the alert, so almost all of the observed silence predates the page. A gap that is already present half an hour before onset looks more like a standing export gap than a sudden outage. It is not a brief blip either — the hole covers the entire half hour.
sections.heading: First look: traces from the front door

sections.body:
Error-ratio baselines were requested for all four services. All four failed, and they failed for the same reason, which turned out to be the single most useful negative result of the investigation: the error-ratio template reads span-derived metrics, and the metrics backend holds no span-derived series for any of these four services because none of them emit traces that get converted into metrics.

This is unavailable, not zero. Three tempting misreadings were explicitly set aside. It does not mean nginx-web-server was healthy and error-free. It does not mean compose-post-service suffered a traffic collapse. And it does not indicate a monitoring pipeline outage coincident with the incident, because the same emptiness covers the one-hour baseline window before onset just as completely as it covers onset itself.

The operational consequence for the next responder: do not re-run these. No choice of window, baseline or service spelling will make this metric family resolve for these four services. Request rate, status-code breakdown including 499s, and upstream latency all remain entirely unmeasured and must be pursued through logs or caller-side instrumentation.

This also corroborates the trace finding. If nginx-web-server emits no traces that become metrics, the empty trace window is comfortably explained as instrumentation coverage rather than as evidence of an outage.
sections.heading: Metrics: four services, four structural dead ends

sections.body:
The log query against nginx-web-server was the one dispatch that could have separated the candidate mechanisms. It never ran. The log backend rejected it with an HTTP 400 — a client-side bad request, with the pod label matcher regex and its escaping the likely culprit.

Three conclusions were ruled out here. The empty frame does not mean nginx logged no errors; nothing was ever retrieved. The log backend is not down — it answered at the application layer with a 400, which is what a reachable, parsing service does; a dead backend would have surfaced as a timeout, connection error or 5xx. And the time range was not the limiting factor, since explicit start and end nanosecond bounds were carried in the request and the rejection happened before they mattered.

This is the highest-value retry available. A corrected pod matcher against the same window answers, in one shot, what every other channel failed to answer: whether the process stalled, whether it lost its path to a backend, whether it ran out of space, or whether its configuration was wrong.
sections.heading: Logs: one bad matcher cost us the decisive answer

sections.body:
Change history was requested for all four services over the twenty-four hours ending at the alert. All four queries died identically — a parse error on an unterminated string partway through the response payload, at the same line and column each time. The response was truncated or malformed during serialisation; the backend never reported zero matching changes.

So the empty flags on these four results carry no weight at all. It would be a serious mistake to record that the change log is clean and exclude deploys, configuration edits or image/tag changes as the trigger. A change-driven cause remains fully open and entirely unexamined.

The repeatability of the error across four separate service names suggests the tool or its upstream data is currently emitting malformed output generally, not that one query was unlucky. A straight retry may reproduce it. Alternate sources worth reaching for: deployment pipeline records, image registry history, and the configuration repository's commit log.
sections.heading: Change history: the same failure four times

sections.body:
Not established. Confidence low. No fix class identified. No evidence gathered during this investigation points at a failing mechanism in any of the four services, and the one genuine observation we have is ambiguous between an outage and a telemetry gap — with the geometry of its window, and the metrics backend's own account of these services' instrumentation, both tilting toward the gap.

Three questions remain open, in priority order. First: what does nginx-web-server's own log say around the alert? Re-run the log query with a corrected pod matcher; this single answer is the discriminator. Second: did nginx-web-server emit traces earlier in the day? If it did, the empty half hour becomes incident evidence instead of an instrumentation artifact, and the first reading of the trace result gains weight. Third: what actually changed on any of the four services in the preceding day, and what signal fired the alert in the first place? We never established the latter, which in hindsight should have been question one.
sections.heading: Where this stands

sections.body:
Two patterns here will recur and are worth internalising.

An errored query and an empty query look alike in a results table and mean opposite things. Four change-history failures and four metric failures all surfaced with empty payloads; none of them was a negative finding. Check for an error string before you write anything down as ruled out.

And a failure that is structural is worth more than a failure that is transient, because it tells you where not to spend the next hour. The metrics backend's explanation — these services do not feed the span-metrics path — permanently closes that route for this part of the topology, and that is a fact worth carrying into the next incident in this namespace rather than rediscovering.
sections.heading: Notes for whoever picks this up

proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is continued customer-visible impact if a real fault is active and untreated at the front door; nginx-web-server is the seed and alerted service, so whatever fired at 05:12:35 keeps firing. That risk is accepted because the alternative is worse: a speculative restart of nginx-web-server would discard its caches and reset every in-flight connection on the only ingress path, and if the true fault is a network partition, a filled disk, or a bad config, the restart either does nothing or returns the service to the same broken state while destroying the process-state evidence (open sockets, file descriptors, memory) that the pending Loki query is meant to read. A rollback or config revert on a service whose change history was never successfully read could install an arbitrary, possibly older-and-worse, image or point a dependency address somewhere stale.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if the corrected Loki query returns nginx error lines clustered at 05:12:35 naming a specific upstream, or if a Tempo query over an earlier same-day window shows nginx-web-server emitting spans normally — either would convert the empty window into onset evidence and localise a mechanism, at which point restart_service on the named service becomes defensible. It is also wrong if the change-log tool recovers and shows a deploy or config edit on one of the four services inside the window, which would make rollback_image or revert_config the right class. Note that abstention's correctness cannot itself be confirmed by a metric: there is no series that goes green to prove not acting was right, which is part of why acting here would be unverifiable too — with span metrics structurally absent for all four services [tr_ecf722d4c88a, tr_df4845357d16, tr_ff29c4182d6f, tr_0a142cfdc055], no permitted action's effect could be measured as an error ratio falling or a latency percentile returning.
proposal.blast_radius: Nobody sees a change, because nothing changes. For contrast, had an action been proposed: a restart or rollback of nginx-web-server would be seen by all external clients, as it is the seed and alerted front door, and by compose-post-service, home-timeline-service and user-timeline-service as dropped inbound connections during the recreate. An action on any one of those three candidate_cause services would be seen by nginx-web-server, which is their named inbound caller, and through it by external clients on the affected request paths.
proposal.expected_effect: No action proposed, so no effect is expected or claimed. Concretely: every permitted action fails its preconditions. rollback_image and revert_config both require a prior image tag or configuration recorded in change history and evidence of a deploy/config change inside the window — all four change-history dispatches died with the same response-parse error [tr_7c7136d87842, tr_53f4cca39479, tr_f3ae6788e684, tr_06833e7a95d8], so no prior tag or config is known to exist and no change is named. restart_service requires evidence pointing at process state; the only observation that ran is zero spans for nginx-web-server across 04:42:35-05:12:41 [tr_3c7a09c7f07e], a window lying almost entirely before the 05:12:35 alert, and the same source rules out reading an empty trace window as either health or outage. The Prometheus results [tr_ecf722d4c88a] establish that this silence is equally consistent with a standing export gap — nginx-web-server emits no traces that become metrics at all. The Loki query that would discriminate process_freeze from network_partition, disk_fill and bad_config was rejected with HTTP 400 for a malformed pod matcher and never executed [tr_ae542892c038]. scale_service, reconnect_service, restore_store and free_storage are listed UNAVAILABLE and cannot be proposed regardless. The next step is investigative, not remedial: re-run the Loki query with a corrected pod label matcher, and query Tempo for nginx-web-server over an earlier window on 2026-10-02 to learn whether this service ever emits spans.
